items.question: How do you think better AI models can change the way drug discovery works?
items.object: AI models and the drug discovery workflow
items.answer: I think this notion of target discovery and hit discovery and optimization, where each of these has a gate and takes a few months to a few years, is this very waterfall model, where the cost of trying things and getting things early is very expensive. But I think if you start to get in a regime where you can have models give you really promising candidates, you can start to make that look a lot more like a loop. It's akin to becoming more agile in software development. But now the next problem is agonists: how do you reliably one-shot hitting a switch on a cell? Or bispecifics or ADCs? And I think these levels of abstraction that we're going to have to climb with the product as the models get better. If you have these really good primitives for structure prediction and binding and design and you can kind of compose them, then you can start to grow into the outer loop of science.

items.question: How has your interest in working on the physical world evolved over your career?
items.object: Working on the physical world versus software
items.answer: I have a more meandering path. I got into programming 15 years ago, making apps in the App Store. Got really addicted to the dopamine hits you get from that, and then actually got nerd-sniped by robotics and worked on that for a bit. Self-driving cars in 2018, 2019. Got really jaded and was like, I don't want to touch hardware for a while. Ended up switching and joining a SaaS company called Vanta as one of the first employees there and kind of grew with it. Started my own security company afterwards. Got a few years into that and I was like, you know what, atoms are kind of cool. I want to work on something a little more meaningful, and so I joined Chai about a year ago, right after Chai 2 was announced, to help with a lot of the platform and commercialization pieces.

items.question: How do you see Chai Discovery’s role in helping pharmaceutical companies develop medicines?
items.object: Chai Discovery’s role in drug discovery
items.answer: As you all know, drug discovery is a very lengthy process, and a lot of these pharma companies are spending years and years and billions of dollars trying to find initial therapeutic candidates. At Chai, we train models that can help accelerate that process and find those initial binders and then some. There's a lot of bio companies, AI for bio companies, that are making their own drugs. We really don't see ourselves that way. We see ourselves as almost a neutral software factory for making medicines. That's what lets us go work with and support all of these other pharma companies in their drug discovery journey. A lot of this capital is just another proof point that we can start to really accelerate that software factory, go after harder modalities, train bigger models, and ultimately build what our partners and customers ask us for.

items.question: Why do you see Chai 2 as a turning point from a product perspective?
items.object: Chai 2's transition into a useful product
items.answer: I think Chai 2 is where it started to get really fun from a product perspective. With Chai 2 we crossed the threshold of usefulness, where after we released that paper we had a lot of pharmas and biotechs approach us and say, “Hey, this model might be able to do some stuff for us. Can we use it?” And then we're like, oh man, we should build a product, something to let you use that model. That's right around when I joined, and there was this mad buildout to both build the product, which we can talk about the shape of, and also go and secure the compute so we can serve those models to our partners.

items.question: How do you think a neutral medicine-design platform can work for an industry as sensitive to intellectual property as pharma?
items.object: Security and intellectual property in a shared medicine-design platform
items.answer: We want to be a very neutral platform that anyone can design medicines on, but pharma is this notoriously IP-sensitive industry. When I joined, a lot of people told me this can't be done. They're not going to put their data in a platform and have all their new medicines be generated out of it. Having a bit of a background in security helped a bit. No, actually, if you are really aggressive about how you segment data and set up single tenancy, where you're almost deploying a separate version or separate account in the product per customer, you can actually build a platform and ship it to them. Through the summer of last year we started doing that. We'd been working with Eli Lilly, and they were one of the first partners to really work with us closely on that, and made that V1 of that design suite that you can use to engineer some of those molecules on.

items.question: Why do you favor a visual design suite for working with Chai's molecular models?
items.object: The visual interface of Chai's molecular design suite
items.answer: I think we have these really powerful models now that can do all of these crazy things if you condition them in the right way, if you give them the right context about the structure that you're going after or maybe the constraints around the model. “Hey, I want to design an antibody that hits this GPCR protein, but doesn't collide with the cell membrane and also targets the specific epitope on that as well.” We looked at it and were like, I guess we could put a chatbot around it. That'd be really easy to talk to, but you're trying to build something almost very visual. You can finally build something really visual with some of these structure prediction models. If you look at the Chai product, it looks a lot less like a ChatGPT and a lot more like Autodesk or SolidWorks or Figma, if you've used those things where you can load up your molecule. There's this almost Photoshop-esque design suite. You have an equivalent of a paint tool to paint your epitope. There's an equivalent of a content-aware fill tool to get your binders generated from Chai. You of course have a lot of the scientific analysis and plotting to understand the results of the models. We've been surprised at how much complexity is in doing that, so that you don't shoot yourself in the foot when you're prompting these models to give you advice.

items.question: How do you think about convincing skeptical pharma scientists to use Chai’s AI models?
items.object: Pharma scientists’ willingness to adopt Chai’s AI models
items.answer:
I think pharma is incredibly pragmatic, actually. It helps a lot to have the models working really well. When we had the results of Chai 2 and Chai 2.5, that's enough of an activation energy where pharma companies and the scientists within these companies are like, “Oh, let's try it. Can Chai, can you guys just try running the model against a few of these targets and let's look at the results?” Then we do that and the results are good, and they're like, “Okay, let me try to get on that product and let me try to use it.”
I've been very impressed with everyone that we've worked with so far. They're willing to be proven wrong, and I don't blame them for not trusting the models. I have used these models, and rightly so, I am pretty skeptical when I see a new release. I always have been. You really just need to show them the proof. They can give you this target that they are interested in, or maybe it's more something they've worked on in the past. They probably don't want to share IP right out of the gate, but they can be like, “Hey, I've had trouble with this particular target in the past. Let's see how you guys can do on this.” Once you show them the proof, they almost overwhelmingly are willing to accept that.

items.question: What do you value about working with pharmaceutical scientists as customers?
items.object: Collaborating with pharmaceutical scientists as product customers
items.answer: I come from a cybersecurity background, or have worked on security products before, and those were dark years because you spend a lot of your time selling to people who are surprisingly not that technical. You think cybersecurity people are very technical; in many cases they're not, and it is this uphill enterprise slog to this very unsophisticated customer. We've been pleasantly surprised at how much I enjoy working with our partners and customers. These are scientists who have been spending 5, 10, 20 years of their life working on one target, often, and they've studied everything about it. They're very sophisticated, very smart. Getting to collaborate with them is a gold mine, and we learn a lot about how to make the product better. There's this anecdote. A few months ago we were showing some of the results from a target with a pharma partnership, and one of the scientists in the room started tearing up and crying.

items.question: What do you value about Chai's cross-disciplinary team when evaluating what its models can actually do?
items.object: Chai's cross-disciplinary team and its rigor in evaluating models
items.answer:
One of the things that I really appreciate about Chai is how cross-disciplinary it is. We have people who are maybe engineering experts and less bio experts, like myself. We have great AI scientists—or ML scientists—but we also have a bunch of scientists that we work with and have joined Chai to help us test the limits of the models: see what is Chai 2 actually capable of, what targets can it do, what can't, inform some of the research direction there.
I want to add to that: in the Chai 2 days we started with a bunch of engineers and people who had AI bio experience. We didn't have a hardcore lab scientist, and one of our first hires in that realm was Nathan Rollins, who started working in the Baker lab at 14, graduated from Harvard at 18, and got his PhD by 21 or something like this, in the Marks lab. He was super skeptical about Chai at first. Then the results start to come in; he's like, “Okay, this is kind of interesting. This could work.” Once the Chai 2 results came back, he was like, “I need to bulletproof this. Nobody celebrate yet.” It's been really nice to have that level of rigor, to have people who have spent the time in the lab, designed proteins themselves, literally—in the case of Andy—led several therapeutic programs, brought drugs to the clinic themselves. We have all these people internally at Chai using the product and really battle-testing that.

items.question: How do you reconcile Chai Discovery's research goal of one-shot drug design with building products for iterative experimentation?
items.object: Chai Discovery's one-shot drug design research and iterative product workflows
items.answer:
I think this notion of target discovery and hit discovery and optimization, where each of these has a gate and takes a few months to a few years, is this very waterfall model, where the cost of trying things and getting things early is very expensive. But I think, to what Matt's saying, if you start to get in a regime where you can have models give you really promising candidates, you can start to make that look a lot more like a loop. It's akin to becoming more agile in software development.
Internally, we kind of have two north stars. At first pass, they almost sound contradictory, but the north star in research is to start to de novo one-shot better and better medicinal candidates that are as close to being ready for the next phase as possible. But also within product we do want to expand into whatever these iterative workflows look like, where maybe I get a binder, I get some results from the lab, I'm using that to condition my next run of the model. They sound contradictory, but I think they're actually not, because what's going to happen is the research is going to get better at identifying a de novo candidate for a specific class of drugs, say antagonists, blocking things, a little bit easier maybe. We can get to a state where we can one-shot pretty good drugs there. But now the next problem is agonists: how do you reliably one-shot hitting a switch on a cell? Or bispecifics or ADCs? There's kind of these levels of abstraction that we're going to have to climb with the product as the models get better.

items.question: How do you think about building molecular design software when improving AI models could make its current features obsolete?
items.object: The lifespan and evolution of molecular design software as AI models improve
items.answer: One of the things—I got very existential a few months ago, because I was like, man, all this stuff we're building in the product to visualize molecules, maybe I'm just going to have to throw it all away when Matt ships Chai 4. But I think that's the reality of building products now. You're using them less as an end in and of itself. Maybe you'd have built software that was supposed to last 20 years. Now it's supposed to last maybe one year, but it is the bridge to deliver value and enable the research that then gets you to the next thing. I'd imagine we're probably going to rewrite our product at higher and higher levels of abstraction. Maybe right now we have something a little bit more akin to Cursor, where you're inspecting the molecule in the same way you're inspecting the code because you really need to verify the bonds that are forming and the properties of the things that you're getting. Then you get to a point where that stuff is solved enough where the product is actually just helping you orchestrate these campaigns of hypotheses. Maybe you have one target and you're orchestrating a bunch of different epitope choices or whatever against that. Then maybe you're going up one level of abstraction where you're doing a whole campaign against all of the targets within a pathway. I think what's really exciting about that is if you have these really good primitives for structure prediction and binding and design and you can compose them, then you can grow into the outer loop of science. Maybe the thing runs itself, and you start to get some really, really cool drugs at the end of it.

items.question: How do you see the challenge of compute infrastructure for startups?
items.object: Compute infrastructure for startups
items.answer: I mean, that would have been my answer: the infrastructure part. Not to beat a dead horse, but compute, getting the compute and using it in the right way, is such a challenge, especially for startups.

items.question: What did trying to secure compute for Chai teach you about the GPU market?
items.object: GPU supply concentration and startup access to compute
items.answer: September of last year, we started to really notice things were getting tight. We were doing a lot of our inference on spot and on-demand markets, and we'd have these days where you just get these capacity crunches, and we're like, okay, we should probably start to get ahead of buying some compute for ourselves. I think everyone probably says this, but man, it was hard. I didn't realize how much of a power law this is, where there's, say, 10,000 B300 units that are shipping everywhere. The hyperscalers and the biggest AI labs are buying 95-plus percent of it, and then you have the startups fighting over the scraps.

items.question: How do you see the compute industry's focus on LLMs affecting the models you build at Chai?
items.object: The compute industry's emphasis on LLM workloads
items.answer: The other thing that's really interesting, especially if you look at these later compute versions, the Vera Rubins or the B300s, a lot of this stuff has been built very LLM-forward. You have systems with huge KV caches where you have 72 GPUs that are all required to talk to each other. Obviously some performance gains there help us, but it's interesting how much the compute market has gotten LLM-pilled. There's probably a whole set of compute stack and inference optimizations and things that need to be made for this class of models. This class of models is going to be just as big, just as impactful as LLMs, but it's almost like the compute kind of doesn't realize that yet, both in the capacity sense and in the software stack sense. We spend a lot of our time doing basic optimizations of compute to get them to work better for the types of models that we have.

items.question: Why do you see durable execution as a foundational engineering problem for Chai?
items.object: Durable execution and Temporal in Chai's compute infrastructure
items.answer:
When you're designing a molecule on Chai, it's not necessarily one call; it's a lot of GPUs being thrown at the problem across a lot of compute. One of the hardest things to get right in software engineering is durable execution. If you're computing a lot of data, model calls across a very wide set of infrastructure, you always run into problems where some part of the infrastructure is flaky. Maybe the bucket you're grabbing your data from goes down, or your database has a blip because there are too many transactions against it, or your GPU errors out. I've been at companies before where you spend so much time dealing with this. You're putting all of these queues and retries and duct-taping things together, and it becomes a mess where what used to be a pretty simple computation that's just distributed, you're spending 95-plus percent of your time on queuing and retry stuff.

We're huge fans of this company called Temporal. There's this idea: if you're trying to get a really long-running job to run, what do you need? You need a queue, your flaky thing pulling off the queue, retry logic to put things back on the queue if they fail, and an orchestration system to tie all the queues together and monitor them. Temporal is a company that's kind of invented a framework for doing this. One technical decision we made early on that was very helpful was to run as much stuff as we can on Temporal. Whether those are calls out to the database from the app, to make sure the database transaction goes through without failing, let's have side effects sit on Temporal so they get retried smartly without us having to write our own queue logic, or things related to model calls or orchestrating really long data pipelines. You need to get durable execution right so you're not stuck in retry hell. A deep engineering thing that you wouldn't realize unless, for me and Jack, you've been burned by this many times before.

items.question: Why do you favor simplicity in research model architectures such as AlphaFold 3?
items.object: Simplicity in research model architecture
items.answer: I have an analogous tangent on the model side. One thing that's nice about those problems is they're super visible. You see, hey, this crashed, this failed; we see the loss curve didn't go down or weird gradient behavior. A lot of these same principles, engineering first, also apply on the research team. One thing that I like to say is complexity and being bitter-lesson-pilled are fundamentally at odds. For example, AlphaFold 3, I might get this number wrong, but I think it was 23 submodules. At that point that's a difficult system to optimize and study. What happens if I tweak this thing in submodule 30 or 21? What happens to the whole system? You can think, hey, we can make this better by adding module 24, but should you, or should you think about removing things and lowering that complexity? That's a fundamental thing at Chai: the engineering culture and being simplicity-biased. Have you all seen the picture of the SpaceX engines? Raptor 1 has a bunch of pipes, and Raptor 2—we have a picture of that on our office wall, because it's just true. How do you delete more things?

items.question: How do you see commoditization affecting the value of frontier models in protein design?
items.object: Commoditization and frontier models in protein design
items.answer: I think the answer is it's kind of all of the above. There probably will be some commodity layer for certain types of modalities or drugs. At the same time we're going to be able to do even more ambitious drugs, and it's just like what's happened in LLM land. You have your open-source models that are maybe general and helpful for some things, but people are still buying frontier models. If you look at the amount of value captured, it's the closed-source frontier models. The whole pie is growing so fast that even as the open-source model share expands, the frontier models are still able to capture the majority of the value. If you have more intelligence, you're going to go after harder tasks. If we have more intelligent biomodels, we're going to go after more crazy bio tasks.

items.question: Why do you consider the product layer around biological models as important as the models themselves?
items.object: The product layer around biological models
items.answer: A lot of the reason I don't use the open-source model is because I don't get Claude Code, I don't get Claude. I think there's a product layer to be built that's just as important as the model layer. We learn a lot from our partners and the people in the building about the really tough things that they get stuck on using the models. Some of them are the dumbest things, like, I want to better visualize this piece and focus on that. Some of them are sophisticated things that we then have to build some pretty vertical product for. Maybe in the fullness of time AGI one-shots everything and it doesn't matter, but I think there's quite a bit of time until we get there, and the product makes a huge difference.

items.question: What do you see as the barriers to generating drug molecules that are almost ready for the clinic in one shot?
items.object: Data and technical barriers to zero-shot drug design
items.answer: I think biology is slow, which is one nice thing, and there's not that much labeled data. You could take all the publicly available sequence information out there that might give you a good base model, but you still need some measurements on that data. That's pretty time-consuming, and then you need to iterate on that. I think there are data blockers into unlocking zero-shot design candidate, generating molecules that are almost ready to go into the clinic. There's more to that than AGI might solve right away. There are definitely technical blockers.

items.question: What do you value about Chai Discovery’s partnership model with pharmaceutical companies?
items.object: Chai Discovery’s partnership model
items.answer: Chai definitely has no plans of starting a pipeline. We take the partnership model pretty seriously. From a personal stance, I love the incentive alignment: we make the models better, the partners succeed more, and that iterates on itself. That's a unique part of Chai: being able to partner with a lot of people and getting feedback on the product, knowing that it's very real. This is in legit big pharma hands, and they're actually running campaigns on this stuff. We have to be model-forward, model-focused; we need to keep delivering value. That puts a lot of pressure on the research team and product team to serve these things. The research teams always shoot for better versions.

items.question: How do you think about the claim that Chai Discovery’s partnership strategy leaves it without a data moat?
items.object: Model progress and data advantages at Chai Discovery
items.answer: The way I think about this is if you're a bitter-lesson-pilled forward kind of thinker or company, then there comes a point where there's a lot to do on both the model and data side, but I don't think either is exhausted. It would be stupid to say we don't need any more data, but also stupid to say the models are stuck and we can only use data to solve these problems. There's tons of room to grow on both sides. We're taking both seriously. I would also push back on the no-data-moat premise. That'd be kind of like saying, hey, all the enterprises that work with Anthropic, you're not letting Anthropic train on your data, so you can't build models that are good at enterprise workflows. We are investing in this. There are ways to turn compute into data and get more, and we're doing those. But what is the kind of data that you're trying to get? What's cool about working so closely and supporting so many of these partners is we learn what would be helpful in research. Rather than doing research in a vacuum based on what would hypothetically be cool, we're able to do informed research based on what our partners have organically been asking us for help with.

items.question: How do you see computational models changing the way biology can be engineered?
items.object: Biology’s transition toward computational precision engineering
items.answer: I think biology has been this somewhat obscure-feeling field where you're stumbling around in the dark. You don't know what you're looking at. You're dealing with non-determinism in your experiments. You're having to do a very long and iterative trial-and-error loop across a very long amount of time. At some point you're crossing that threshold of what you can do computationally, when you can get folding models down to being within an angstrom, where you can get design models to give you hit rates north of 50%, where now you can put them in a 96-well plate and actually have 48 interesting binders. You start to get to the point where now you can declaratively precision-engineer what you want rather than betting on nature or trial and error to get you there. We had the same thing happen in software, where you can write code and deterministically get an outcome, or in electrical engineering, where instead of your schematic being drawn out, you can put it in Cadence Design Systems and get it made in software, or CAD for mechanical engineering, where you can precision-engineer your part and get it printed or manufactured. The same thing is happening in bio, and it's happening very quickly.
